title: The Briefing: Did Man City save the title race? Can Romero lead? Is an old-school tactic returning?
content:
Welcome to The Briefing, where every Monday during this season, The Athletic will discuss three of the biggest questions to arise from the weekend’s football.

This was the round when Chelsea’s Cole Palmer started to shine again, Keith Andrews continued to make a mockery of those of us who thought Brentford had taken a huge risk by appointing him as head coach in the summer, Manchester United reeled off a fourth successive victory, and Liverpool suffered more stoppage-time despair.

We will ask, after a wild game at Anfield on Sunday, whether Manchester City have just saved the title race, how highly Cristian Romero scores on Vincent Kompany’s leadership scale, if a type of cross from yesteryear is making a welcome return and, finally, search for answers that are impossible to find to one of the most curious pieces of Premier League defending.

It was over. Bernardo Silva knew that and so did his Manchester City team-mates.

With less than 10 minutes of normal time remaining, Manchester City were trailing Liverpool 1-0 and the gap at the top of the table was a huge nine points. Pep Guardiola slumped into his seat after Dominik Szoboszlai scored a remarkable free kick that meant every bit as much to Arsenal as it did to Liverpool. Erling Haaland shook his head. Gianluigi Donnarumma looked stunned.

But there was a twist, and the sort of twist that makes you think about words such as fate and destiny, and whether this will go down as one of those season-defining matches. It was that kind of game at Anfield, and that kind of ending, as Manchester City snatched victory from defeat in extraordinary circumstances.

Silva, who was like a man possessed throughout (more about what teams should expect from captains later), understood the significance. It was there in how he played, it was there in how he reacted to his equaliser — no celebration, just a rush to get the ball back on the centre spot as soon as possible — and it was there in his words after the final whistle.

“I feel that the whole team knew before the game that if we lost this game, probably the title race is over,” he told Sky Sports.

It was such a dramatic victory that it’s easy to lose sight of the fact that Arsenal are still in a commanding position. Mikel Arteta’s side are out in front, six points clear with 13 games remaining, and with a superior goal difference. On top of that, City are the only team in the top six that Arsenal still have to play away from home.

Psychologically, though, this felt like a big moment, not just because City won the game but because of how City won. They looked beaten and broken until Silva — who else? — latched onto Haaland’s header to score a goal out of nothing.

As for the winner, Arsenal supporters, and not just Liverpool fans, will wonder why Alisson had a rush of blood that led to him bringing down Matheus Nunes in stoppage time and Haaland, showing nerves of steel, converting from the spot.

Arsenal — and this will be the message from inside Arteta’s camp — have to focus purely on their own games, performances and results. Everything else is outside of their control and a waste of emotional energy.

That said, it is inevitable that minds will wander. This was one of the games where Arsenal would have hoped City might slip up. They had won at Anfield on just three occasions since 1953, and Guardiola’s only victory came during Covid, when the stadium was empty. Szoboszlai’s wonder goal pointed to a familiar script.

Instead, Guardiola’s team can now move to within three points of Arsenal if they beat Fulham at home on Wednesday. Fulham, for the record, have lost their past 18 games against City in all competitions, the longest losing run that one side has had against another in English football history.

Arsenal, with their glass-half-full mentality, might think that dreadful sequence has to come to an end sometime.

Either way, this title race has a way to go yet.

Society has changed over the past couple of decades, and so, it follows, the modern-day footballer has changed, too — and that extends to what a captain looks like.

Managers appoint leadership groups these days, rather than having one individual knocking on their door, which is partly to ensure the dressing room is represented as a whole, taking in everything from different nationalities and cultures to all sorts of personalities.

Perhaps that shift is also a sign that the old-school leader no longer exists. It’s Martin Odegaard wearing the armband at Arsenal now, not Patrick Vieira. It’s Bruno Fernandes at Manchester United, not Roy Keane. It’s Silva at Manchester City, not Kompany. It’s Reece James at Chelsea, not John Terry.

A captain does not have to shout the loudest or fly into every tackle as if their life depends on it. It’s about being dependable, commanding respect, taking responsibility during the good as well as the bad times, and motivating and inspiring those around you, whether that’s with actions or words. In short, a captain can be relied upon.

Some players are captain material from a young age. Others need time to mature and grow into the role. “I say to Bernardo often, ‘You are 50 per cent clown, 50 per cent leader’,” Kompany said in 2019 about the man who was given the armband at City by Guardiola this summer. “When he becomes 25 per cent clown, 75 per cent leader, he will become the captain of this team.”

Revisiting that comment on the back of Silva’s brilliant performance against Liverpool makes you wonder: what percentage ‘leader’ is Romero at Tottenham Hotspur?

“He leads from his behaviour on the pitch, driving the team forward in every way, and outside the pitch he’s always pushing the team,” Thomas Frank said in August, when he announced the decision to appoint Romero, who had previously been one of two vice-captains at Spurs.

Six months later and Romero faces a four-match ban, his third suspension of the season, following his second red card of the campaign — and all at a time when Tottenham, who are seven games without a win in the Premier League and only six points above the drop, need leadership on the pitch more than ever.

Romero, of course, is not the reason Spurs are in a relegation battle — that’s a whole different conversation that points to a lack of leadership elsewhere in the club, something the Argentine has waded into through a combination of interviews and social media posts, much to the delight of the club’s supporters. “Romero is right, the board is s***e,” sections of the fanbase sang during defeat against Manchester United at Old Trafford.

Holding the board and owners to account is all well and good (I wish some of the captains of the club I support had done that kind of thing at times to represent the anger and frustration we felt as fans), but speaking out does not give Romero, or anyone else wearing an armband, a free pass on the pitch.

Romero, for all his obvious talent, experience and success with his country, is a danger to his own team at times. A liability, even. Aged 27, he is prone to moments of recklessness and what you might describe as head loss — something that seems to have caught Frank by surprise.

“If you look at his record, he’s not actually getting that many cards,” the Spurs head coach said after the 2-0 defeat at United. A reporter politely pointed out to Frank that Romero has received the most red cards in the Premier League since he joined Spurs in 2021. “OK. I didn’t know that,” Frank replied.

He does now, and that must leave him questioning his judgement back in the summer. As for Romero, he will be hoping his Spurs team-mates can bail him out over the coming weeks.

There is something about seeing a cross swung in from deep, from a winger or a full-back’s natural side, and being met with a first-time finish. It feels like a bit of a throwback to days gone by, when delivering a curling ‘same side’ cross into that area between the goalkeeper and the defence (no, I’m not using the phrase corridor of uncertainty) was encouraged at every opportunity.

Three goals were scored that way on Saturday in the Premier League, with Brentford’s Vitaly Janelt, West Ham United’s Valentin Castellanos, and Manchester United’s Fernandes the chief beneficiaries.

In the case of Brentford’s Dango Ouattara and West Ham’s El Hadji Malick Diouf, their assists were more eye-catching than the goals themselves because of the way in which both players crossed the ball so invitingly, with a mixture of conviction and precision, and also from so far back.

To say that Janelt and Castellanos only had to get their head on the ball would be unfair, but in both instances it’s the kind of cross that a player attacking the box dreams of receiving and, in the same breath, a nightmare for the retreating defence. David Beckham comes to mind.

In the modern game, where so much emphasis out of possession is on forcing opponents wide and stopping them from playing through the middle of the pitch, space often opens up on the flanks. Typically, though, it is inverted wingers receiving in those positions and that, naturally, means the ball is often funnelled infield.

Interestingly, Michael Carrick set up with Patrick Dorgu and Amad on their natural side in his first game as Manchester United manager, against Manchester City. Later in that game, Matheus Cunha came on for United and delivered a cross from the right that Dorgu converted from a near-identical position to the one that Fernandes took up to score his goal against Spurs, almost ghosting into the penalty area on the blind side of opponents.

Attackers will only make those runs if they know there is a good chance the ball will be delivered — something that was almost guaranteed when Ouattara, a natural left-footer, scampered into the left channel at Newcastle on Saturday.

Ouattara’s cross was, in the words of Brentford head coach Andrews, “sensational” — and that was not hyperbole.

At the same time, it did not escape The Briefing’s notice that the Newcastle right-back Kieran Trippier barely raised a leg to try to block the cross (a bugbear for some people with full-backs now), almost as if he was quite happy for Ouattara to cross a ball from that position.

A few years ago, I got into a debate about this topic with a colleague, who pointed to the data that showed how few goals are scored from crosses as a reason for full-backs to be relaxed about balls being delivered from wide areas. Maybe that school of thought will change if the line on the chart below continues to move in an upward direction.

What on earth was going through Lucas Digne’s mind? A couple of his Aston Villa team-mates, Emiliano Buendia (arms outstretched) and Douglas Luiz (head in his hands), looked like they were asking themselves the same question after Digne bizarrely — and it really was bizarre — allowed the Bournemouth winger Rayan to breeze past him before shooting inside the near post to equalise in the teams’ 1-1 draw.

It was such a strange passage of play and genuinely hard to make sense of what had happened, other than to say that Digne, inexplicably, turned into a training-ground mannequin.

Initially, he was showing Rayan wide — the natural thing to do in the one-vs-one scenario that he found himself in — but as soon as the Brazilian came inside, the Villa left-back seemed to give up. He turned 180 degrees so casually and slowly that he might as well have been waving Rayan on through.
